title: A chapter a day
hook: most Bible-reading habits are small: one chapter, same time, every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, two testaments, and your line: the story began long before. Did you read the six verses of Psalm 1? Today, how people actually keep reading. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

January first. A fresh start, and a big resolution: this is the year I read the whole Bible, cover to cover. You start at Genesis. Creation, the flood, Abraham, Joseph: it's great. Exodus: plagues, the sea splitting, even better. Then, around February, you reach Leviticus. Chapter after chapter of rules for sacrifices, skin diseases and mildew. And somewhere in there, the bookmark stops moving. If that's happened to you, you're in very large company. Here's what people who've read the Bible for decades tend to say: the grand plan isn't what lasts. What lasts is small. One chapter. Same time. Same chair. Every day. Today's word is that habit.
screen: `THIS IS THE YEAR.` → `LEVITICUS, AROUND FEBRUARY.` → `THE BOOKMARK STOPS.`

segments.voice: A chapter a day. The idea is old. In the book of Acts, the people of a town called Berea are praised because they "searched the scriptures daily." Daily. Not in one heroic weekend. God tells Joshua, "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." A little, often. Here's some math. The Protestant Bible has about eleven hundred and eighty-nine chapters. At one a day, that's a little over three years for the whole thing. Most chapters take three or four minutes to read. About as long as this lesson. Here's a surprise: chapters aren't original. The biblical writers didn't use them. The chapter divisions most Bibles use were added in the thirteenth century, and verse numbers came even later, in the 1500s. They're handles, not part of the text. Christians have built all kinds of plans on those handles. A Scottish minister in 1842 made a plan that took his congregation through the whole Bible in a year, at four chapters a day. The Book of Common Prayer takes Anglicans through all hundred and fifty psalms every month. Catholics hear scripture on a set cycle of readings at every daily Mass, and many Protestants use reading plans on their phones. And if you're starting from nothing, many pastors and priests give the same advice: don't start at Genesis. Start with a Gospel. Mark is the shortest, sixteen chapters. Sixteen days, and you've read a whole account of the life of Jesus. Missed a day? The plan doesn't care. Pick it up where you left off. Small and daily wins.
screen: `THEY SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY.` · `ABOUT THREE YEARS, ONE A DAY.` · `CHAPTERS CAME LATER.` · `START WITH MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your time and your place. Settle, and breathe. Picture your ordinary day. Where is there four minutes that's already yours? Morning coffee. The bus. Lunch. Right before bed. Pick one. Now pick the place: a chair, a corner, a seat on the train. See yourself there with a Bible, or an app, open to Mark, chapter one. If you pray, you can offer that time to God before it starts. If you don't, simply decide it's yours. The bell holds the time.
A chapter a day. The small, steady habit most lifelong Bible readers keep: one chapter, same time, every day. Today's word.
Your line: small and daily wins. Today, read one chapter at the time and place you chose. Mark chapter one is a good door. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 127 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP FOR MY FEET (PSALM 119:105)`

howItsDone: Many Christians read a chapter or a set passage of the Bible every day, often with a reading plan, a daily devotional or the church's lectionary, at a regular time such as early morning or before bed.

notes: 1,189 chapters in the 66-book Protestant Bible (929 OT + 260 NT): confirm.
Chapter divisions credited to Stephen Langton (early 13th century); verse numbers to Robert Estienne (NT 1551). Confirm.
M'Cheyne's plan (1842): Old Testament once, New Testament and Psalms twice in a year, about four chapters a day. Script simplifies to 'the whole Bible in a year'. Confirm.
BCP 1662 appoints the Psalter to be read through each month at Morning and Evening Prayer. Confirm.
Leviticus 'mildew' (Leviticus 13–14, leprosy in garments and houses; KJV 'fretting leprosy'). Informal description. Confirm tone.
'Many pastors and priests suggest starting with a Gospel': common advice, not a rule.
